chem-molecules-basics: When two or more atoms lock together, they form a molecule — and molecules are the true actors in chemistry. Two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen make water; a few dozen carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms make sugar; millions of repeating units make plastic. The same handful of elements, endlessly rearranged, build everything from air to your DNA.
chem-covalent-bonds: A covalent bond is two atoms sharing electrons — the chemical equivalent of holding hands with the same pair of marbles. Oxygen shares two pairs with two hydrogens to make water, and carbon shares four bonds in endless variety. These shared-electron bonds are the strongest and most common in organic chemistry, and they're why molecules have such stable, specific shapes.
chem-ionic-bonds: An ionic bond forms when one atom fully hands an electron to another — sodium gives one to chlorine, and the resulting opposite charges snap together into a crystal. That's table salt, and it's why salts are brittle, melt at high temperatures, and dissolve in water: the ionic lattice is a grid of pure electrical attraction. Ionic compounds are what make seawater taste salty.
chem-metallic-bonds: In a metal, atoms don't share electrons in pairs — they donate them to a shared 'sea' that flows freely between all the atoms. That electron sea is why metals conduct electricity and heat so well, why they're malleable and ductile, and why they shine: free electrons absorb and re-emit light. Bend a paperclip and you're testing a metallic bond.
chem-hydrogen-bonds: A hydrogen bond is a weak attraction between a hydrogen atom in one molecule and an oxygen or nitrogen in another — far weaker than a real bond, yet it runs the living world. Hydrogen bonds make water liquid instead of a gas, hold DNA's two strands together, and fold proteins into the shapes they need. Life is a story of gentle attractions.
chem-water-polar-molecule: Water's oxygen pulls shared electrons harder than its hydrogens, leaving one end of the molecule slightly negative and the other slightly positive — a lopsided charge that makes water polar. That polarity is why water dissolves so much, why it beads on wax, and why it clings to itself. Every property that makes water essential to life traces back to this one-sided tug-of-war.
chem-water-surface-tension: Surface tension is the invisible skin on water: molecules at the surface cling sideways and downward to each other so tightly that a water strider can stand on it and a carefully placed paperclip can float. The skin comes from hydrogen bonds pulling water molecules together. Soap destroys it, which is why bubbles and detergents work.
chem-capillary-action: Capillary action lets water climb against gravity — in a thin tube, the water's attraction to the walls plus its own surface tension pulls it upward. Plants rely on it to lift water from roots to leaves that can be a hundred meters up. It's also why paper towels soak up spills and why a straw's water curves up at the edges.
chem-water-universal-solvent: Water is called the universal solvent because its polar molecules can pull apart and surround more substances than any other liquid — salts, sugars, acids, and most of the chemistry of life. Blood, sweat, coffee, and the sea are all water doing its dissolving job. The catch: water also dissolves pollutants and carries them everywhere, which is why clean water is hard to keep clean.
chem-ice-floats: Almost everything shrinks when it freezes — but water expands, which is why ice floats. In liquid water, molecules pack tightly; when it freezes, they lock into a hexagonal lattice with more space between them, making solid water less dense. That quirk means lakes freeze top-down, fish survive under the ice, and ice cubes bob in your glass instead of sinking.
chem-boiling-points: Boiling happens when molecules gain enough energy to break free of the liquid and escape as vapor. Water boils at 100°C at sea level, but boil it in Denver and it's done at 95°C — lower air pressure means less energy needed to escape. Add salt and the boiling point rises slightly, which is why pasta water is salted but also why salt alone won't speed up dinner.
chem-states-of-matter: The same molecules can be solid, liquid, or gas depending on how much energy they have — ice, water, and steam are all H2O, just moving at different speeds. Solids hold shape, liquids flow but stay put, gases expand to fill any container. Add enough energy to strip electrons off atoms and you get a fourth state, plasma — the stuff of stars and lightning.
chem-sublimation: Sublimation is skipping the liquid step: a solid turning straight into vapor, or vapor straight into solid. Dry ice (frozen carbon dioxide) sublimes at -78.5°C, which is why it never leaves a puddle — just fog. Frost on a cold window is deposition, the reverse: water vapor freezing straight to ice crystals without ever being liquid in between.
chem-condensation: Condensation is vapor turning back into liquid — the reverse of evaporation. When warm, moist air hits a cold surface, its molecules lose energy and glue back together into droplets: that's the fog on your cold drink, the dew on grass at dawn, and the steamed-up mirror after a hot shower. It's also the engine of rain, as rising water vapor cools and condenses into clouds.
chem-plasma-state: Plasma is matter so hot that electrons are ripped free of their atoms, leaving a glowing soup of charged particles — it's the most common state of matter in the universe, making up stars, lightning, and the auroras. On Earth we use it in neon signs, plasma TVs, and fluorescent bulbs. It behaves differently from gas because charged particles respond to electric and magnetic fields.
